entry.idea: Nuclear power needs uranium, but mined supplies are limited, so Fluxnium built fibers that pull uranium dissolved in seawater, tapping a nearly endless fuel source.
entry.lesson: When a resource everyone will eventually need is abundant but scattered and hard to reach, building the extraction technology can open a market far bigger than competing for the scarce, easy-to-mine version.
entry.name: Fluxnium

growth.reason: No user, revenue or funding numbers are available in the coverage, and nothing else stands in for growth evidence.

market.reason: Nuclear fuel supply is a large, worldwide industry, since every nuclear plant on Earth needs a steady uranium source.

tech.reason: Extracting uranium directly from seawater with custom fibers is genuinely new science that would take a strong team years to match.

sources.title: Clean tech startup Fluxnium found a way to tap 50,000 years' worth of nuclear fuel
US firm eyes 4 billion tons of ocean uranium for 50,000 years of fuel

entry.twist: The ocean is estimated to hold about 4 billion tons of dissolved uranium, so this fiber technology could unlock roughly 50,000 years' worth of nuclear fuel.
entry.who_pays: Nuclear power plant operators and utilities that need a long-term, reliable supply of uranium fuel.
entry.why_now: Interest in nuclear power as a steady, low-carbon energy source is rising just as mined uranium supplies stay limited, making a cheap way to pull it from seawater valuable now.

mentions.snippet: Fibers that extract uranium directly from seawater, a nearly endless nuclear fuel source.
